analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security and SSI payments for a year and cuts taxes on benefits for middle-income retirees.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2020 with one cosponsor, the bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have corrected a scheduled drop in Social Security benefits caused by the wage-index formula, then added a one-year across-the-board increase, a higher minimum benefit for people with lifetime low earnings, larger benefit checks for widows and widowers in two-income households, and child benefits extended to age 23 for full-time college students. It also would have loosened eligibility for Supplemental Security Income for 2020 and raised the income levels at which Social Security benefits become taxable. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and was never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Current Social Security and disability beneficiaries, who would get a one-year bump in checks and protection from a formula-driven benefit cut; retirees with lifetime low earnings, who would get a higher minimum benefit scaled to years worked; widows and widowers; students through age 23 whose deceased, disabled, or retired parent's benefits would continue; children living with grandparents or other relatives; and aged, blind, or disabled people with low incomes, whose SSI income and savings limits would be temporarily raised. Middle- and upper-income retirees would also pay less tax on their benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security and SSI recipients, low earners, students

how_it_helps.text: Changes the benefit formula so that new retirees do not get a smaller benefit because pandemic-era wage declines lowered the National Average Wage Index used in the calculation [S3].
Raises the first benefit formula factor from 90 percent to 93 percent for 2020, recomputing every beneficiary's payment, and pays for the increase out of the general Treasury fund [S3].

Creates a new minimum benefit for 2020 tied to the poverty line and scaled up with years worked, reaching a quarter of the poverty guideline at 14 years of work and more at longer careers, aimed at people with lifetime low earnings [S3].

Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for single filers and $50,000 for joint filers, reducing federal income tax on benefits for middle- and upper-income retirees [S3].
Lets children of deceased, disabled, or retired workers keep receiving benefits through age 23 while in full-time college, instead of losing them at 18 [S3].
Raises SSI's income and savings limits for 2020 only, temporarily letting more aged, blind, and disabled people with very low income qualify [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The general fund of the Treasury, and ultimately general taxpayers, would cover the benefit increases through appropriations to the Social Security trust funds, with the trust funds held harmless so the money comes from general revenue rather than payroll taxes. Higher-income retirees would forgo some of the tax the current law collects on their benefits, made up by the general fund.

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the general fund to pay for the benefit increases and to make the trust funds whole for the revenue lost from the lower benefit taxation, adding to federal borrowing during a period of record pandemic deficits [S3].

Nearly all of the benefit increases apply only to calendar year 2020, so recipients would face a drop-off the following year, which the bill itself requires the Social Security Commissioner to account for when recomputing payments [S3].

The tax change in the bill reduces the portion of Social Security benefits counted as taxable income, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge as a permanent reduction in a revenue source that currently helps finance Medicare and Social Security, offset here by general-fund transfers [S3].

A fair objection: one-year, emergency-style changes to retirement benefit formulas create administrative complexity, with the bill requiring recomputation of every primary insurance amount for a single year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets, the gains are real and immediate: protection from a formula-driven benefit cut, a one-year raise in checks, and a higher floor for lifelong low earners. The costs are general-revenue spending during a deficit-heavy year and a permanent tax break on benefits for retirees above the new thresholds, which shifts financing away from a progressive-ish tax on benefits toward general borrowing. The design is a blunt emergency tool rather than durable reform, but its costs fall broadly on taxpayers rather than on the recipients it helps.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in early December 2020, sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, and stayed there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Senator Hirono introduced the bill on December 9, 2020, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the bill's final congressional action [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no vote ever held in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody's benefits changed, but the parties better positioned by the bill's death are general-revenue taxpayers, who avoided the appropriations, and higher-income retirees, who kept the current taxation of benefits unchanged rather than facing a bill that would have, on net, cut their benefit taxes. The Social Security trust funds also avoided a new claim on general revenue, and no industry was materially affected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers and no one's benefits changed

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional Senate support it attracted

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no committee or floor vote ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have raised the income thresholds for taxing benefits, cutting federal income tax for retirees above $35,000 (single) or $50,000 (joint), while requiring general-fund transfers to keep the trust funds whole for the lost revenue. That shifts the cost of the tax cut to general taxpayers, the opposite direction from the bill's benefit increases for low earners.
The bill holds SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries harmless from any benefit changes so states' eligibility determinations are not disrupted, sparing state budgets administrative churn.
